text: In Nazareth, Jesus stopped reading mid-sentence, at "the acceptable year of the Lord." You live inside that comma.
explanation:
Isaiah 61 says the Messiah would come "to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord, and the day of vengeance of our God." When Jesus read it aloud in the synagogue, He stopped right after "the acceptable year of the Lord," closed the book and sat down.

Between that comma and "the day of vengeance" lie two thousand years of grace. This is the season of God's favour, when the good news goes out to every nation. Jesus knew exactly where to stop, and so should we: today is not a day of wrath for you, but the year of His welcome.

text: You're not waiting for the Antichrist. You're waiting for Jesus.
explanation:
The grace of God teaches us to live "looking for the blessed hope and glorious appearing of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ." The blessed hope isn't a terrifying figure or a time of catastrophe; it's a Person.

"Having now been justified by His blood, we shall be saved from wrath through Him." The cross already absorbed God's wrath against your sins. So when you read the news and the world grows darker, lift your head. Your Saviour is coming for you.

text: "I will come again and receive you to Myself, that where I am, there you may be also."
explanation:
Jesus spoke these words in the upper room, hours before His arrest. He was the one about to be betrayed and crucified, yet He was comforting the disciples who would soon run away: "Let not your heart be troubled."

In a Jewish betrothal, the bridegroom went away to prepare a home for his bride, then came back to fetch her, at a day and hour she didn't know. Jesus has gone to prepare a place for you in His Father's house. He isn't coming to deal with your sins; He dealt with them once for all. He's coming for His bride.

text: "The Lord Himself will descend." Not an angel, not a messenger: Himself.
explanation:
Paul could have written simply "the Lord will descend." Instead, the Holy Spirit chose "the Lord Himself." It's a word of warmth that runs through Scripture: "He Himself took our infirmities." On the Emmaus road, "Jesus Himself drew near." "The Son of God, who loved me and gave Himself for me."

The best part of His coming isn't streets of gold or the end of sickness, wonderful as those are. It's this: "and thus we shall always be with the Lord." Heaven wouldn't be heaven without Him, and He's coming in person for you.

text: "In a moment" translates the Greek atomos: an instant so small it can't be divided.
explanation:
"We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet." The word for moment is atomos, the root of our word atom, meaning indivisible. The change will be instantaneous.

This corruptible body will put on incorruption, and this mortal body will put on immortality: no more aging, sickness or fatigue, and no more stumbling into the things you're ashamed of. Your body is the one part of your salvation still to come, and Jesus has already paid for it.

text: The last time the disciples saw Jesus, His hands were raised, blessing them. He'll return the same way.
explanation:
"He lifted up His hands and blessed them. Now it came to pass, while He blessed them, that He was parted from them and carried up into heaven." The angels then said, "This same Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will so come in like manner."

He didn't leave scowling or with a warning finger raised. He left with His hands stretched out over His people, and He hasn't lowered them since. That's how He wants you to picture Him today: blessing you, loving you, always.

text: It's not the sheep's job to take care of the shepherd. "The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not lack."
explanation:
Sheep aren't known for their brains, but they are loved, fed and protected, as long as they stay with the shepherd. There's no such thing as a wild sheep; a sheep was never meant to look after itself.

God knows the cares on your shoulders and your daily responsibilities. Come under His care and let Him be your Shepherd. When the Lord is your shepherd, the next words follow as surely as night follows day: you shall not lack.
